island.quest.title: Borrow the strategy, not the picture
island.quest.tip: Lui often leaves wide blank space and dense ink. Van Gogh uses urgent crossing strokes and complementary colour. The point is how they handle feeling, not copying a whole picture.
island.quest.q: To show pressure with a breath of space, which move is real transfer?
island.quest.a: Paste the whole Starry Night picture, then add a lotus.
island.quest.b: Use urgent strokes for anxiety, then spare space and one bright accent to breathe.
island.quest.c: Copy both artists' biographies and birth years.
island.quest.ok: Well done — you took the problem-solving move, not a surface collage.
island.quest.missA: Try again: pasting the whole picture stays on the surface. Pull out stroke and blank-space strategies.
island.quest.missC: Try again: biography matters less. Look at form and your own transfer.

island.mq.research.title: Which set counts as primary evidence?
island.mq.research.context: Strong workbooks use your own looking, a survey you made, site photos, and lived experience. Web images and news alone are usually second-hand.
island.mq.research.q: Which set is closer to primary evidence?
island.mq.research.a: Find ten stress pictures online and fill the page.
island.mq.research.b: Seven days of your own photos, a classmate survey, and site poses you shot.
island.mq.research.c: Ask AI to write an 800-word essay that students are stressed.
island.mq.research.ok: Well done — primary evidence comes from what you did and saw yourself.
island.mq.research.missA: Try again: web images are usually second-hand. Shoot, ask, or note it yourself.
island.mq.research.missC: Try again: an AI essay is not your observation, and it is not the art process.
island.mq.critique.title: Upgrade casual talk into clear critique
island.mq.critique.sub: Dark and messy colours → clear, still readable
island.mq.critique.context: This picture is so dark and black, and the lines are a mess. It feels awful to look at.
island.mq.critique.a: The colours are very gloomy, the painter was messy, and it is scary.
island.mq.critique.b: Low-value, low-chroma cools, urgent crossed strokes, and a tight crop build pressure.
island.mq.critique.c: This is an oil painting with black, deep blue, grey, and many lines.
island.mq.critique.ok: Well done — you named how value, chroma, and stroke carry the feeling.
island.mq.critique.missA: Try again: skip vague messy or scary. Name the visual elements.
island.mq.critique.missC: Try again: that line stays on the surface. Say how the elements build the mood.
island.mq.sba.title: Which reflection sounds real?
island.mq.sba.sub: A failed test and the change
island.mq.sba.context: Write what you tried, how it failed, and what you changed. Empty phrases do not show the work was yours.
island.mq.sba.q: Which paragraph fits a process reflection?
island.mq.sba.a: "This piece grapples with the profound metamorphosis of urban alienation..."
island.mq.sba.b: The oil-pastel sheet fell off white glue (test A). Hot glue held (test C), and deeper shadow on the features increased the pressure.
island.mq.sba.c: I had fun, used acrylic and a board, and hope people like it.
island.mq.sba.ok: Well done — you named the trial, the failure, and the change.
island.mq.sba.missA: Try again: vague phrasing does not prove the process. Rewrite the steps you actually tried.
island.mq.sba.missC: Try again: add how you solved the picture or material problem.
island.mq.exam.title: Shared first, then contrasts
island.mq.exam.sub: Two figure sculptures — practice structure, no paper IDs
island.mq.exam.context: First write what they share (subject, medium), then contrast form, space, tone, and movement. Do not finish one image before the other.
island.mq.exam.a: Spend most of the time on image one, and two lines on image two.
island.mq.exam.b: Shared: both are figure or family sculptures. Contrast: one is rounded with negative space; the other is geometric and pushes forward.
island.mq.exam.c: Only say which one you prefer, with no formal analysis.
island.mq.exam.ok: Well done — shared traits and contrasts are both there.
island.mq.exam.missA: Try again: cross-compare both images. Do not write one out fully first.
island.mq.exam.missC: Try again: a preference needs formal analysis behind it.

lesson.f4u3l3.title: November: Getting to know community art — research
lesson.f4u3l3.subtitle: In class, learn what community art is, with past cases for reference. You do not need to go out and run a project.
lesson.f4u3l3.card.theme.body: A community-art theme comes from a real setting — people, places, habits and objects. Start in the classroom, the canteen, the school gate, the way to school, or a memory, and choose one nearby detail to look at.
lesson.f4u3l3.card.observe.body: Use sketches and notes to look at a nearby detail: a corner of the classroom, a canteen seat, the school gate, the way to school, or a memory. Ask permission before photographing people, and respect privacy.
lesson.f4u3l3.card.interview.body: A short classroom interview can ask a classmate which thing in the classroom, the canteen, the school gate, or the way to school they usually do not notice. Keep the questions short, leave pauses, and note the key sentences.
lesson.f4u3l3.card.insight.body: Take one nearby insight from the classroom, the canteen, the school gate, the way to school, or a memory: a detail you had not noticed before that relates to the community. Write clearly what you see, and why it relates to the place and the people.
lesson.f4u3l3.card.practice.body: This lesson is for recognising community art in class. The visual diary continues each week. Practice starts from a nearby detail, for appreciation and insight. The class does not use a real exam paper.
lesson.f4u3l4.title: November: Getting to know community art — develop and make
lesson.f4u3l4.subtitle: In class, look at past cases, then use a classroom exercise to turn that recognition into making. You do not need to go out and run a project.
lesson.f4u3l4.card.make.body: Use a material trial to turn a nearby insight into a making exercise — paper, a pen, clay, or other classroom materials. Write down which materials and skills you use.
lesson.f4u3l4.card.three.body: Use three sentences for how you tried materials: the theme, how you made it, and what you want the audience to feel. Check the short criteria, then self-assess or ask a classmate to write one sentence.
lesson.f4u3l4.card.practice.body: This lesson practises ways to develop and make in class, with a material trial and a three-sentence talk. The class does not claim an official public-exam result.

unit.header.stage.label: Learning stage / year
goal.appreciate: Developing the ability to appreciate art
unit.f4u1.theme: The course and the SBA portfolio
unit.f4u1.themeMessage: Meet the two learning strands (appreciation and making), and the basic SBA portfolio structure. Lessons only teach structure and method.
unit.f4u2.themeMessage: First build a foundation in looking and materials, practising observational drawing, composition, aesthetics, design thinking and material exploration, before theme-based making.
unit.f4u4.theme: Self-portrait, artist research and theme development
unit.f4u4.themeMessage: Use self-portrait to explore identity, and practise proper artist research, to start developing a theme. You can begin from self, relationship and story.
unit.f4u5.themeMessage: Use a short timeline and keywords to practise looking at form, function and cultural context. This is an introduction only.
unit.f4u6.themeMessage: From everyday objects and experiences, draw out topics that can keep exploring a theme.
unit.f4u7.theme: Visual presentation of a theme and appreciation writing
unit.f4u7.themeMessage: Only the structure is taught: how appreciation writing is organised, how theme exploration unfolds, and how you choose a medium and a way of presenting. Lessons do not use real exam papers.
unit.f5u1.theme: Public-exam structure and the visual diary
unit.f5u1.themeMessage: Review the two learning strands (appreciation and making), learn the structural difference between the two public-exam papers, and continue the weekly visual diary. Lessons only teach structure and method.
unit.f5u2.theme: Chinese and Western aesthetics and Song–Yuan art
unit.f5u2.themeMessage: Ask how “beauty” can be understood in Chinese and Western societies, then use a short timeline to begin Song–Yuan art. Practise looking at form, function and cultural context.
unit.f5u3.themeMessage: Starting from how heritage and society shape everyday life, practise gathering materials, developing a theme, and trying ink and mixed media.
unit.f5u4.themeMessage: Learn traditional colours, patterns and symbols in painting, and practise describing the form you see and a possible symbolic meaning.
unit.f5u5.theme: Role-taking: re-presenting a person in a Chinese context
unit.f5u5.themeMessage: Practise how to re-present a person in a Chinese context, and use a research-and-making structure to develop the work.
unit.f5u6.themeMessage: Learn about contemporary Chinese calligraphy currents, make an introductory comparison with global contemporary art, then practise innovative heritage.
unit.f5u7.themeMessage: Look back on a year of learning: what is going well, what can still improve, and how to write a short portfolio overview.
unit.f6u1.themeMessage: Continue the weekly visual diary, and use a structure to check and organise the portfolio. Lessons only teach method.
unit.f6u2.themeMessage: Use a short timeline to begin Ming–Qing aesthetics, and compare Young British Artists (YBA) with related contemporary approaches. This is an introduction only.
unit.f6u3.themeMessage: Start from everyday life, learn related artists and symbols, then develop work in ink and mixed media.
unit.f6u4.themeMessage: Extend the observation of traditional symbols, and begin literati painting. Practise describing form, brush and ink, and a possible symbol.
unit.f6u5.theme: Role-taking: re-presenting in a Chinese context
unit.f6u5.themeMessage: Practise role-taking and re-presenting identity, and develop work with dry and wet media.
unit.f6u6.themeMessage: Review the Form 6 portfolio: look at your strengths and next steps, and write a short overview.
lesson.f4u1l1.part.element: When looking at a work, record the form you see: line, shape, colour, symbols and style.
lesson.f4u1l1.part.principle: Organise the form you see together with the historical, social or cultural context of the work.
lesson.f4u1l1.part.appreciate: Object of appreciation: one work or image seen in class. Focus of appreciation: how form and cultural context appear together.
lesson.f4u1l1.part.expression: Turn experience, feeling or thought into a visual form you want to try.
lesson.f4u1l1.part.making: On the left, record the form and context you see; on the right, record the materials and steps you want to try.
lesson.f4u1l2.part.element: In the research workbook, record the form you see in theme exploration, related works and media trials.
lesson.f4u1l2.part.principle: Under the same theme, organise how the research workbook and the artwork / critical studies support each other.
lesson.f4u1l2.part.appreciate: Object of appreciation: one work or one critical-studies page in the portfolio. Focus of appreciation: how the theme is presented, and what evidence shows the learning process.
lesson.f4u1l2.part.expression: Use the artwork / critical studies to say your visual expression of this theme.
lesson.f4u1l2.part.making: Open the research workbook by structure: gather materials, try a medium, and write a reflection on progress. Lessons only teach structure.
lesson.f4u1l3.part.element: For each keyword, write one definition and one formal example you see in a work.
lesson.f4u1l3.part.principle: Describe the form first, then use the keyword to explain how you understand the work.
lesson.f4u1l3.part.appreciate: Object of appreciation: two examples you choose for the same keyword. Focus of appreciation: which example makes the meaning clearer.
lesson.f4u1l3.part.expression: Use keywords to write how you understand the work.
lesson.f4u1l3.part.making: Use your own keyword cards to organise the definition, the example, and how you will use it in appreciation writing. This lesson only practises structure.
lesson.f4u1l4.part.element: For each art movement, write one formal feature and one way of presentation.
lesson.f4u1l4.part.principle: Arrange the movements in an order you can compare, and look at how form meets the audience.
lesson.f4u1l4.part.appreciate: Object of appreciation: one way of presentation from each of two art movements. Focus of appreciation: one similarity and one difference, without only memorising dates.
lesson.f4u1l4.part.expression: Use the timeline to say the points you choose, rather than filling every period.
lesson.f4u1l4.part.making: Use your own cards to organise period, formal feature and way of presentation. Do not copy a real exam paper.
lesson.f4u2l1.part.element: In observational drawing, first look at overall shape and proportion, then add line, shape, colour, texture and space.
lesson.f4u2l1.part.principle: Try contrast, rhythm, balance and emphasis, or a rule of thirds, a diagonal leading line, or negative space, to organise the picture.
lesson.f4u2l1.part.appreciate: Object of appreciation: Wucius Wong’s way of bringing design principles into ink landscape. Focus of appreciation: how structure helps you organise the picture.
lesson.f4u2l1.part.expression: Use a large shape, proportion, and one leading line to say where you want the audience to look first.
lesson.f4u2l1.part.making: Use writing and your own line drawing for one exercise: large shape, proportion, and one leading line.
lesson.f4u2l2.part.element: Try pencil, charcoal, ink or collage, and record the texture and colour of the material.
lesson.f4u2l2.part.principle: Follow design thinking: define the problem, propose options, try, reflect, and improve.
lesson.f4u2l2.part.appreciate: Object of appreciation: two material studies of the same everyday object. Focus of appreciation: which material better expresses your theme and intention.
lesson.f4u2l2.part.expression: Say the theme clearly, why you chose this medium, and how the audience can read your composition and symbols.
lesson.f4u2l2.part.making: Choose one everyday object, draw or make it once in each of two materials, and record limits and feeling in writing and samples.
lesson.f4u2l4.part.element: In the drawing, mark the viewpoint, a sense of scale, and which element carries the message.
lesson.f4u2l4.part.principle: First define the problem, then draw options, then present them through a material trial.
lesson.f4u2l4.part.appreciate: Object of appreciation: your design-drawing proposal this time. Focus of appreciation: how material limits change your way of presenting.
lesson.f4u2l4.part.expression: Say in three sentences: the problem, the option you chose, and how the material helps the message.
lesson.f4u2l4.part.making: When choosing a material, write down limits such as foldable, transparent, thick or light, then run a trial.
lesson.f4u3l1.part.element: Use composition sketches and colour notes to record the line, shape, colour and texture you see.
lesson.f4u3l1.part.principle: One entry in four columns — date, place, one observation, and a sketch — helps you organise what you see each week.
lesson.f4u3l1.part.appreciate: Object of appreciation: one entry in your visual diary. Focus of appreciation: how observation and composition present what you saw and felt that day.

lesson.f4u4l1.part.principle: Starting from self, relationship or story, organise how symbols come together as a picture that speaks about yourself.
lesson.f4u4l1.part.appreciate: Object of appreciation: one approach by Frida Kahlo, Ho Sin-han or Hockney related to self-portrait, role or family gaze (described in writing from a reliable source). Focus of appreciation: how symbols speak about the self or a relationship.
lesson.f4u4l1.part.expression: Use a self-portrait to say how you see identity or relationship; the point is not likeness alone.
lesson.f4u4l1.part.making: Organise your own sketches and writing; describe contemporary works in writing and note a museum page or a reliable encyclopaedia.
lesson.f4u4l2.part.element: When looking at related works, record the form, then connect it to a visual emphasis in your own theme.
lesson.f4u4l2.part.principle: Organise by steps: choose a related artist, record facts, look at form and context, connect to the theme, and write a view with evidence.
lesson.f4u4l2.part.appreciate: Object of appreciation: the approach of one or two artists compared in your briefing. Focus of appreciation: how their methods connect to your question that explores a theme.
lesson.f4u4l2.part.expression: Use the first briefing to say the question that explores a theme, your starting angle, and the medium you want to try next.
lesson.f4u4l2.part.making: The research workbook should show drafts, trials, failures and improvements. Use museums, textbooks or teacher notes as sources.
lesson.f4u4l3.part.element: Compare new trials with older drafts, and point out which visual emphasis you changed.
lesson.f4u4l3.part.principle: The second briefing should show process: older drafts, new trials, and one sentence on why you changed.
lesson.f4u4l3.part.appreciate: Object of appreciation: the artist method you cite again in the second briefing. Focus of appreciation: how you adapt this method.
lesson.f4u4l3.part.expression: Say your current question that explores a theme, the new evidence, and the next work.
lesson.f4u4l3.part.making: Use the research workbook to show your own development. Speak only about your own process.
lesson.f4u5l1.part.element: For cave images, notice animals, handprints, space and repetition; for Egypt, profile view and hierarchical scale; for Greece, body proportion and balance; for Rome, portraiture and public architecture.
lesson.f4u5l1.part.principle: Use a short timeline to compare the problems different periods used images to solve: recording, belief, power or commemoration.
lesson.f4u5l1.part.appreciate: Object of appreciation: one image or way of presentation organised in class for each of the four periods. Focus of appreciation: how form and function correspond.
lesson.f4u5l1.part.expression: For each of the four periods, write one keyword plus one sentence on function.
lesson.f4u5l1.part.making: Organise form, function and context in writing; this can become a group art dictionary or a personal timeline. This is an introduction only.
lesson.f4u5l2.part.element: Recognise line, symbols and negative space in pictographs, oracle-bone script or bronze patterns.
lesson.f4u5l2.part.principle: Look at how calligraphy and painting use brush movement, negative space and rhythm to organise a picture.
lesson.f4u5l2.part.appreciate: Object of appreciation: one early image, pattern or calligraphy-and-painting example (as a line drawing or a written description). Focus of appreciation: form and possible context.
lesson.f4u5l2.part.expression: In short sentences, say the line you see and a possible meaning.
lesson.f4u5l2.part.making: Choose one pictograph or object pattern, draw it once in your own line drawing, then write two sentences of observation.
lesson.f4u5l3.part.element: For Qin–Han, look at mural narrative and clerical-script line; for Wei–Jin, look at early Dunhuang story scenes, Gu Kaizhi’s line figures, and the brush rhythm of Wang Xizhi’s calligraphy.
lesson.f4u5l3.part.principle: Describe line, density, and how figures are placed in space.
lesson.f4u5l3.part.appreciate: Object of appreciation: one mural, line-figure or calligraphy example you choose in the Qin–Han to Wei–Jin introduction. Focus of appreciation: how line and space organise a scene.
lesson.f4u5l3.part.expression: Write the form you see in short sentences. This is an introduction only.
lesson.f4u5l3.part.making: Organise observations with your own line drawing or a written description. Museum pages may be used only as classroom reference.
lesson.f4u5l4.part.element: For Tang, look at composition and near-and-far in figures, landscape or calligraphy; for Five Dynasties, look at landscape texture strokes and layers of ink.
lesson.f4u5l4.part.principle: Use line, ink, negative space and near-and-far to separate foreground, middle ground and distance.
lesson.f4u5l4.part.appreciate: Object of appreciation: one landscape, figure or calligraphy example you choose in the Tang to Five Dynasties introduction. Focus of appreciation: how composition and ink separate near and far.
lesson.f4u5l4.part.expression: Use a few technical words to describe the form you see.
lesson.f4u5l4.part.making: Organise with writing and your own small study. Do not copy a famous painting as homework.
lesson.f4u6l1.topic.collection.label: Collection
lesson.f4u6l1.topic.family.label: Family object
lesson.f4u6l1.topic.conflict.label: Conflict
lesson.f4u6l1.topic.collection.part.elem: Sort a small box of curious collections — tickets, stones, packaging or old objects — and record shape, colour, texture and traces.
lesson.f4u6l1.topic.collection.part.prin: Start from one real object, and put the object, one question and a next step in the same column.
lesson.f4u6l1.topic.collection.part.appr: Object of appreciation: one collected object you kept. Focus of appreciation: how form and traces speak about a side of you.
lesson.f4u6l1.topic.collection.part.expr: Ask why you kept it, and which side of you it speaks about.
lesson.f4u6l1.topic.collection.part.maki: Use a worksheet to write the object, one question and a next step. The topic should be small and real.
lesson.f4u6l1.topic.family.part.element: Choose one family object, and record its shape, material, and traces of use.
lesson.f4u6l1.topic.family.part.principl: Organise who uses it, when it is used, and whether there is a rule or a memory, as evidence of a relationship.
lesson.f4u6l1.topic.family.part.apprecia: Object of appreciation: the family object you choose. Focus of appreciation: how the object speaks about a relationship.
lesson.f4u6l1.topic.family.part.expressi: Use this family object to write a relationship question you want to keep asking.
lesson.f4u6l1.topic.family.part.making: Use a worksheet to write the object, one question and a next step.
lesson.f4u6l1.topic.conflict.part.elemen: From a minor character’s viewpoint, sketch a scene of crowding, waiting, rules or misunderstanding, including figures and space.
lesson.f4u6l1.topic.conflict.part.princi: Record the scene and the feeling side by side, and see where the tension appears.
lesson.f4u6l1.topic.conflict.part.apprec: Object of appreciation: one conflict or tension scene you sketched. Focus of appreciation: how figures and space present the tension.
lesson.f4u6l1.topic.conflict.part.expres: Write the question you want to keep asking in this scene.
lesson.f4u6l1.topic.conflict.part.making: Use a sketch and a worksheet to record the scene, one question and a next step.
lesson.f4u6l2.part.element: Look at the form in the materials you have already gathered, and point out which visual emphasis can drive further looking.
lesson.f4u6l2.part.principle: Follow the briefing outline: the topic, the question that explores a theme, materials already gathered, and the next medium.
lesson.f4u6l2.part.appreciate: Object of appreciation: your existing materials, together with a question that explores a theme. Focus of appreciation: what the question wants to pursue, and what the materials show.
lesson.f4u6l2.part.expression: Turn the topic into a question that explores a theme; the question should drive looking, research or a media trial.
lesson.f4u6l2.part.making: List the materials you already have, and choose the medium you want to try next. This lesson only teaches structure and method.
lesson.f4u6l3.part.element: In an extension, decide which visual element carries a surreal or abstract picture; for a wish, say which element carries the “what if”.
lesson.f4u6l3.part.principle: Whether you extend, wish or assemble, return to the original question that explores a theme.
lesson.f4u6l3.part.appreciate: Object of appreciation: the extension, wish or assembly trial you choose. Focus of appreciation: how the new presentation still answers the original question that explores a theme.
lesson.f4u6l3.part.expression: Write three sentences: the original question that explores a theme, the presentation you changed, and one visible piece of evidence.
lesson.f4u6l3.part.making: An assembly may use found scraps, paper and your own images; record why each material is there. You may try two combinations.
lesson.f4u7l1.part.element: In appreciation writing, first describe the form you see, then analyse the organisation.
lesson.f4u7l1.part.principle: Appreciation can take four parts: describe form, analyse organisation, interpret a possible meaning, then make a judgement with evidence. Theme exploration unfolds by the question, the materials, one artist method, and a visual emphasis.
lesson.f4u7l1.part.appreciate: Object of appreciation: one work or image provided in class under a question outline you draft yourself. Focus of appreciation: form, organisation and a possible meaning. Practice structure · not a real paper.
lesson.f4u7l1.part.expression: Use the exploration section to say how your own question unfolds.
lesson.f4u7l1.part.making: Practise writing structure with a question outline you draft yourself. Do not use a real exam paper.
lesson.f4u7l2.part.element: Try the same theme sentence once in each of two media, and compare which form is clearer.
lesson.f4u7l2.part.principle: Making structure in four steps: one theme sentence, the audience, the choice of medium, and the way of presenting.
lesson.f4u7l2.part.appreciate: Object of appreciation: two media trials of the same theme. Focus of appreciation: how object, function, form and material are presented together. Practice structure · not a real paper.
lesson.f4u7l2.part.expression: Use the four steps to say how you want the audience to read this theme sentence.
lesson.f4u7l2.part.making: Choose two media, try each once, and write which is clearer. Only structure is taught.
lesson.f5u1l1.part.element: When reviewing, describe the form you see; when making, choose one medium and try one small step.
lesson.f5u1l1.part.principle: Learn separately the structure of the two public-exam papers: Paper 1’s requirements for a two-dimensional work, and Paper 2’s design submitted to the brief. Lessons only teach structure.
lesson.f5u1l1.part.appreciate: Object of appreciation: one two-dimensional or design image provided in class. Focus of appreciation: form and a possible cultural context. Do not use a real exam paper.
lesson.f5u1l1.part.expression: Practise the two learning strands side by side: appreciation writes form and context; making writes the step you want to try.
lesson.f5u1l1.part.making: Choose one medium and try one small step. Lessons only teach structure and method.
lesson.f5u1l2.part.element: A page can have a sketch, one observation, and one still-open question.
lesson.f5u1l2.part.principle: Records can be organised by form, possible use, and the medium you want to try next week.
lesson.f5u1l2.part.appreciate: Object of appreciation: one page in your visual diary. Focus of appreciation: how observation and the still-open question drive each other.
lesson.f5u1l2.part.expression: Write what form you saw, and what you want to try next week.
lesson.f5u1l2.part.making: Keep the record in the classroom: use photos already on hand, objects, or materials the teacher provides.
lesson.f5u2l1.part.element: Look in three parts: the form you see, what it is for, and the kind of life it appears in.
lesson.f5u2l1.part.principle: Compare how “beauty” can be understood in Chinese and Western societies: sometimes harmony and character, sometimes personal feeling or formal experiment.
lesson.f5u2l1.part.appreciate: Object of appreciation: one work or image provided in class for comparing Chinese and Western views. Focus of appreciation: form, function and cultural context.
lesson.f5u2l1.part.expression: Be able to say which angle you are using; do not say which society is the correct one.
lesson.f5u2l1.part.making: Use short sentences to write form, function and context separately. This is an introduction only.
lesson.f5u2l2.part.element: Choose one Song or Yuan work, and look at form such as negative space, line, or the proportion of scenery.
lesson.f5u2l2.part.principle: Use a short timeline to compare Song and Yuan; you may set court, literati and popular visual choices side by side.
lesson.f5u2l2.part.appreciate: Object of appreciation: one Song or Yuan work you choose for this introduction (a classroom indication or a written description). Focus of appreciation: form, function, and its rough place on the timeline.
lesson.f5u2l2.part.expression: Be able to say which point you are comparing, rather than memorising every date.
lesson.f5u2l2.part.making: Use a timeline and short sentences to organise the form and function of one work. This is an introduction only.
lesson.f5u3l1.part.element: Start from one everyday object, and record form, colour and arrangement.
lesson.f5u3l1.part.principle: Organise the object’s place in everyday life together with a heritage or social habit.
lesson.f5u3l1.part.appreciate: Object of appreciation: one everyday object, festival colour or home arrangement. Focus of appreciation: how heritage and society shape the way you see this thing.
lesson.f5u3l1.part.expression: Write the influence and feeling you yourself see.
lesson.f5u3l1.part.making: Interview, observation and collecting are all done in class: use a conversation with a classmate, a photo already on hand, or a classroom object.
lesson.f5u3l2.part.element: Look at the outer form and texture of strange-stone images, and at the parts that are exaggerated or cut apart.
lesson.f5u3l2.part.principle: Compare how Wu Bin paints the strange, and how Surrealism or Cubism reassembles what is seen.
lesson.f5u3l2.part.appreciate: Object of appreciation: Wu Bin’s way of painting strange stones, and a Surrealist or Cubist way of reassembling what is seen. Focus of appreciation: where it is exaggerated, where it is cut, and where it is still recognisable as stone.
lesson.f5u3l2.part.expression: Talk about method; do not turn the comparison into a requirement to copy a particular painting.
lesson.f5u3l2.part.making: Compare with a classroom indication and your own sentences; do not copy the picture.
lesson.f5u3l3.part.element: Gather classroom sketches, photos already on hand, interview notes or one object, and record forms that keep returning.
lesson.f5u3l3.part.principle: Collect on one page, then narrow on the next, and choose a repeated interest from the materials.
lesson.f5u3l3.part.appreciate: Object of appreciation: a set of materials in your visual diary used to develop a theme. Focus of appreciation: which interest keeps returning and can be narrowed into one theme sentence.
lesson.f5u3l3.part.expression: Write one theme sentence that says what you want to keep exploring.
lesson.f5u3l3.part.making: Interview, observation and collecting are all done in class.
lesson.f5u3l4.part.element: Use ink, water and paper for small ink effects; try mixed media when needed.
lesson.f5u3l4.part.principle: The first portfolio piece uses a structure: one theme sentence, material evidence, one media trial, and a next step. Change only one condition each time.
lesson.f5u3l4.part.appreciate: Object of appreciation: this ink or mixed-media trial. Focus of appreciation: which effect better suits your theme.
lesson.f5u3l4.part.expression: Use the trial to say the theme, and write a next step.
lesson.f5u3l4.part.making: Try a few small effects and write down the differences. What you submit is your own trial and structure.
lesson.f5u4l1.part.element: Record separately the form you see in traditional colour, pattern and painting.
lesson.f5u4l1.part.principle: Point out whether the pattern is repetition, symmetry, or one object used again and again.
lesson.f5u4l1.part.appreciate: Object of appreciation: one traditional colour, pattern or painted symbol in a classroom indication. Focus of appreciation: the form, and a possible symbolic meaning. Write the estimate as “possible”.
lesson.f5u4l1.part.expression: Use your own description to say what you see, and what you estimate the meaning might be.
lesson.f5u4l1.part.making: Complete everything in class, using a classroom indication and your own description.
lesson.f5u4l2.part.element: Look again at one formal detail of a Song or Yuan work: negative space, density of line, or the proportion of figures to scenery.
lesson.f5u4l2.part.principle: Compare two works for one similarity and one difference.
lesson.f5u4l2.part.appreciate: Object of appreciation: two Song or Yuan works you choose for extended looking. Focus of appreciation: one similarity and one difference.
lesson.f5u4l2.part.expression: Write how this formal detail helps you understand the work.
lesson.f5u4l2.part.making: Complete everything in class with observation and short sentences. The extension is still looking, not practising every technique from the start.
lesson.f5u5l1.part.element: In role-taking, look at clothing, pose and setting, and at which detail accounts for identity.
lesson.f5u5l1.part.principle: When re-presenting in a Chinese context, organise what traditional pose, symbol or scene you borrowed, and what you changed.
lesson.f5u5l1.part.appreciate: Object of appreciation: one image or approach used in class to discuss methods of re-presenting. Focus of appreciation: identity, pose, and how a viewer might understand the person.
lesson.f5u5l1.part.expression: Write what this person is doing in the picture, and which detail accounts for identity. Role-taking is not the same as looking like someone.
lesson.f5u5l1.part.making: Practise with method and your own sentences.
lesson.f5u5l2.part.element: Compare the clear edges of dry media (pencil, pastel, charcoal) with the spread of colour in wet media (ink, watercolour).
lesson.f5u5l2.part.principle: Change only one condition each time: dry or wet, pressure, or how wet the paper is.
lesson.f5u5l2.part.appreciate: Object of appreciation: this dry- or wet-media trial. Focus of appreciation: whether the effect can be used on the clothing or background of the role.
lesson.f5u5l2.part.expression: Write which side you want this effect to re-present.
lesson.f5u5l2.part.making: Try everything in class, and record what you used and what effect you saw.
lesson.f5u5l3.part.element: Take one formal detail from Song–Yuan looking — negative space, line or figure proportion — and use it to develop the role or the picture.
lesson.f5u5l3.part.principle: The second portfolio piece uses a structure: one theme sentence, one piece of research evidence, one dry- or wet-media trial, and a next step.
lesson.f5u5l3.part.appreciate: Object of appreciation: one Song–Yuan formal detail you take into the second piece, together with one media trial. Focus of appreciation: how this detail helps you re-present a person.
lesson.f5u5l3.part.expression: Borrow a method to develop the role or the picture; do not copy a whole picture.
lesson.f5u5l3.part.making: Organise theme, evidence, trial and next step by structure.
lesson.f5u6l1.part.element: Look at how writing becomes visual form: how strokes are repeated or reassembled, and whether the writing is still recognisable.
lesson.f5u6l1.part.principle: Ask how the audience is to look: where to start, and how to follow the strokes.
lesson.f5u6l1.part.appreciate: Object of appreciation: one approach, in Xu Bing or in a contemporary Chinese calligraphy current, that turns writing into visual form. Focus of appreciation: whether the writing is still recognisable, and how the audience is to look.
lesson.f5u6l1.part.expression: Use your own sentences to say the method you have come to recognise.
lesson.f5u6l1.part.making: Finish with classroom writing, an indication diagram, and your own sentences. Learn the method; do not copy the picture of a particular work.
lesson.f5u6l2.part.element: Look at what materials and form a classroom indication uses to speak with the audience.
lesson.f5u6l2.part.principle: Compare whether the material is an everyday object, whether the work needs the audience to come close to see it whole, and whether the title changes your understanding.
lesson.f5u6l2.part.appreciate: Object of appreciation: one global contemporary work indicated in class that you choose. Focus of appreciation: form and one way of looking.
lesson.f5u6l2.part.expression: Be able to say clearly how one work speaks with the audience. An introduction is not the same as knowing every region.
lesson.f5u6l2.part.making: Complete everything in class with an indication and short sentences.
lesson.f5u6l3.part.element: A three-dimensional collage or installation uses materials, writing parts or symbols as a form the audience can come close to look at.
lesson.f5u6l3.part.principle: Add only one material each time, and write which viewing angle it changes.
lesson.f5u6l3.part.appreciate: Object of appreciation: your classroom three-dimensional collage or installation trial. Focus of appreciation: how a symbol or writing method is reassembled, and what the audience sees on coming close.
lesson.f5u6l3.part.expression: Turn a symbol or writing method you have already met into a work the audience can come close to look at. The idea may ask whether writing can still be read, and whether parts can be reassembled.
lesson.f5u6l3.part.making: Complete everything in class. Do not copy a particular work.
lesson.f5u6l4.part.element: Look back at one form from this year: negative space, line, proportion, or one difference among court, literati and popular choices.
lesson.f5u6l4.part.principle: Write one detail into the research workbook, and place it on the same page as theme, evidence, trial and reflection.
lesson.f5u6l4.part.appreciate: Object of appreciation: one Song–Yuan formal detail you observed this year. Focus of appreciation: how this detail helps your making.
lesson.f5u6l4.part.expression: Say how this detail enters your own theme.
lesson.f5u6l4.part.making: Closing is writing it into the workbook, not memorising the timeline again. Complete everything in class.
lesson.f5u7l1.part.element: In review, point out which diary page, trial or work has a form you handled steadily.
lesson.f5u7l1.part.principle: A strength needs one piece of evidence; the next step is only one small action that can be done in class.
lesson.f5u7l1.part.appreciate: Object of appreciation: one practice or trial from your year that has evidence. Focus of appreciation: what is steady, and which step is still messy.
lesson.f5u7l1.part.expression: Use one theme sentence or a short line to say what you want to improve next.
lesson.f5u7l1.part.making: Write only one small action. What you review is your own process.
lesson.f5u7l2.part.element: The overview should be able to say what form or theme the artwork / critical studies present.
lesson.f5u7l2.part.principle: A four-sentence structure: one theme sentence, what the research workbook has done, what the artwork / critical studies present, and what the next step is. The two parts should support each other.
lesson.f5u7l2.part.appreciate: Object of appreciation: the draft of your own portfolio overview. Focus of appreciation: how the workbook and the artwork / critical studies support each other.
lesson.f5u7l2.part.expression: Use four sentences to say a year of learning and the next step.
lesson.f5u7l2.part.making: There is no locked word count. It is enough that each of the four sentences does one job. The overview writes your own structure.
lesson.f6u1l1.part.element: A page can still have a sketch, one observation, and one still-open question.
lesson.f6u1l1.part.principle: Write the learning habit in concrete terms: when you record, how much you record, and what you will ask next week. The habit is repeating these three things.
lesson.f6u1l1.part.appreciate: Object of appreciation: one visual-diary page you are continuing. Focus of appreciation: whether the sketch, the observation and the still-open question appear together.
lesson.f6u1l1.part.expression: Write what you want to ask next week, so the habit is concrete.
lesson.f6u1l1.part.making: Keep the record in the classroom, and continue the weekly visual diary with materials already on hand. Lessons only teach method.
lesson.f6u1l2.part.element: When checking the portfolio, point out the form already present in the theme sentence, research evidence, media trials, and artwork / critical-studies pages.
lesson.f6u1l2.part.principle: Use a list to see what you have and what is missing; organising means grouping materials already on hand.
lesson.f6u1l2.part.appreciate: Object of appreciation: your portfolio materials as they stand now. Focus of appreciation: which item is clear, and which is still missing.
lesson.f6u1l2.part.expression: For the missing item, write only one way to fill it.
lesson.f6u1l2.part.making: The way to fill it must be doable in class. Lessons only teach method, and will not be written as an administrative procedure or a school-year timetable.
lesson.f6u2l1.part.element: Choose one Ming or Qing work, and look at density of brush and ink, amount of negative space, and a possible everyday use.
lesson.f6u2l1.part.principle: Use a short timeline first to know the rough order, then compare whether brush and ink are sparse or dense, and whether the work feels more like self-amusement or more like a social occasion.
lesson.f6u2l1.part.appreciate: Object of appreciation: one Ming or Qing work you choose for this introduction (a classroom indication or a written description). Focus of appreciation: form and a possible everyday use.
lesson.f6u2l1.part.expression: Use short sentences to say the aesthetic choice you see. This is an introduction only.
lesson.f6u2l1.part.making: Organise with a timeline and short sentences. Do not copy famous paintings one by one.
lesson.f6u2l2.part.element: Look at how Young British Artists (YBA) use material, title and setting to speak about identity or the everyday.
lesson.f6u2l2.part.principle: Set this approach side by side with the Ming–Qing looking you have already started.
lesson.f6u2l2.part.appreciate: Object of appreciation: one contemporary approach by Young British Artists (YBA), together with one Ming–Qing observation you already have. Focus of appreciation: how an object is enlarged, or how the everyday is turned into a subject. Write the full name; do not use only the three letters as a title.
lesson.f6u2l2.part.expression: Compare methods, and say how each side handles the everyday or identity.
lesson.f6u2l2.part.making: Complete the comparison with a classroom indication and short sentences. Do not copy a question, and do not use a real exam paper.
lesson.f6u2l3.part.element: Write one formal observation each for Shen Zhou and Wen Zhengming: how rocks are written, the density of trees, or how inscription and picture appear together.
lesson.f6u2l3.part.principle: Compare the two for one similarity and one difference.
lesson.f6u2l3.part.appreciate: Object of appreciation: one introductory example each for Shen Zhou and Wen Zhengming (a classroom indication or a written description). Focus of appreciation: one similarity and one difference.
lesson.f6u2l3.part.expression: Speak about the form you see; do not memorise a full biography.
lesson.f6u2l3.part.making: Organise observations in short sentences. This is an introduction only; do not copy famous paintings one by one.
lesson.f6u3l1.part.element: Start from one object you already use, one festival colour, or an arrangement in the home, and record the form.
lesson.f6u3l1.part.principle: Write three things: the form, where it appears in a day, and which heritage habit you still see.
lesson.f6u3l1.part.appreciate: Object of appreciation: one everyday object, festival colour or home arrangement. Focus of appreciation: how heritage appears in everyday life.
lesson.f6u3l1.part.expression: Write which habit you feel still shapes you.
lesson.f6u3l1.part.making: Interview and collecting are done in class: use a conversation, a photo already on hand, or a classroom object.
lesson.f6u3l2.part.element: Write one formal observation each for Xu Wei, Chen Chun and Tang Yin: speed of the brush, density of flowers and leaves, or whether the inscription or the picture catches the eye first.
lesson.f6u3l2.part.principle: The three may be compared on only one shared point.
lesson.f6u3l2.part.appreciate: Object of appreciation: one introductory example each for Xu Wei, Chen Chun and Tang Yin (a classroom indication or a written description). Focus of appreciation: one shared or different formal choice.
lesson.f6u3l2.part.expression: Speak about the form you see; an introduction does not need a full biography.
lesson.f6u3l2.part.making: Organise in short sentences. Do not copy paintings one by one, and do not use a real exam paper.
lesson.f6u3l3.part.element: Look at the form of a bird, a rock or a signature, and record how it makes you feel what kind of person the painter is.
lesson.f6u3l3.part.principle: Describe the form first, then estimate how the symbol accounts for identity. Write the estimate as “possible”.
lesson.f6u3l3.part.appreciate: Object of appreciation: one introductory example of Bada Shanren (a classroom indication or a written description). Focus of appreciation: the relationship between symbol and identity. Identity is not the same as memorising a life story.
lesson.f6u3l3.part.expression: Say which detail in the picture supports your estimate.
lesson.f6u3l3.part.making: Describe and estimate in short sentences. Do not copy the picture, and do not use a real exam paper.
lesson.f6u3l4.part.element: A figure-painting introduction may look at Chen Hongshou or Wu Bin: figure proportion, drapery line, and how expression is exaggerated.
lesson.f6u3l4.part.principle: Change only one condition in each ink trial. The first portfolio piece uses a structure: one theme sentence, one figure-painting form, one trial, and a next step.
lesson.f6u3l4.part.appreciate: Object of appreciation: one introductory figure-painting example by Chen Hongshou or Wu Bin, together with your ink or mixed-media trial. Focus of appreciation: how the figure form is used in your own theme.
lesson.f6u3l4.part.expression: Decide whether this effect can be used on a figure, and write a next step.
lesson.f6u3l4.part.making: Write down the trial effect. Interview and collecting are done in class.
lesson.f6u4l1.part.element: First describe the form you see in colour, pattern and painting.
lesson.f6u4l1.part.principle: Then write a possible meaning. An introduction may ask whether meaning can be completed by the audience, and whether an object can leave its original use.
lesson.f6u4l1.part.appreciate: Object of appreciation: one traditional symbol in a classroom indication. Focus of appreciation: the form, and one possible meaning.
lesson.f6u4l1.part.expression: Use your own sentences to write the form and a possible meaning. Do not copy a question.
lesson.f6u4l1.part.making: Complete everything in class, using a classroom indication and your own sentences.
lesson.f6u4l2.part.element: A literati-painting introduction may look at dry and wet brush and ink, negative space in the composition, or the relation between the inscription and the picture.
lesson.f6u4l2.part.principle: Compare one related approach of the Four Monks or a related school; speak about method rather than memorising a full list of names.
lesson.f6u4l2.part.appreciate: Object of appreciation: one introductory example of the Four Monks or a related school (a classroom indication or a written description). Focus of appreciation: one form and one possible symbol.
lesson.f6u4l2.part.expression: Speak about one form and one possible symbol.
lesson.f6u4l2.part.making: Complete everything in class with short sentences. Do not copy a public-exam question.
lesson.f6u5l1.part.element: Decide how a person is re-presented: clothing, pose, setting and viewing angle.
lesson.f6u5l1.part.principle: When re-presenting in a Chinese context, you may borrow one traditional pose or symbol, but you must write what you changed.
lesson.f6u5l1.part.appreciate: Object of appreciation: the method used by artists such as Cindy Sherman to discuss identity through role-play, or one classroom re-presentation example. Focus of appreciation: which detail makes the identity be read as another kind of person. Method only; do not copy a question.
lesson.f6u5l1.part.expression: Write which side you want to re-present, and what you changed.
lesson.f6u5l1.part.making: Practise with method and your own sentences.
lesson.f6u5l2.part.element: Write one formal observation each for the Yangzhou Eccentrics, Xu Beihong and Qi Baishi: subject matter, dry or wet brush, or how much negative space.
lesson.f6u5l2.part.principle: Look at the Yangzhou Eccentrics as one group of methods; you do not need to split them into another complete list of names.
lesson.f6u5l2.part.appreciate: Object of appreciation: one introductory example of the Yangzhou Eccentrics, Xu Beihong or Qi Baishi (a classroom indication or a written description). Focus of appreciation: one formal observation.
lesson.f6u5l2.part.expression: Speak about the form you see; do not copy paintings one by one.
lesson.f6u5l2.part.making: Organise observations in short sentences. Lessons do not use a real exam paper.
lesson.f6u5l3.part.element: Compare how dry media more easily hold an edge, and how wet media more easily spread.
lesson.f6u5l3.part.principle: Structure for the second piece: one theme sentence, one identity detail, one dry or wet trial, and a next step. Change only one condition in each trial.
lesson.f6u5l3.part.appreciate: Object of appreciation: one dry or wet trial you made for the second portfolio piece. Focus of appreciation: how this condition serves the person you are re-presenting.
lesson.f6u5l3.part.expression: Write how it serves the person you are re-presenting, and write a next step.
lesson.f6u5l3.part.making: Change only one condition in the trial, and write down the effect.
lesson.f6u6l1.part.element: In review, point out which page of research is clear, and which work still has not spoken the theme.
lesson.f6u6l1.part.principle: A strength needs one piece of your own evidence; the next step is only one action that can be done in class.
lesson.f6u6l1.part.appreciate: Object of appreciation: one researched page or work in your Form 6 portfolio that has evidence. Focus of appreciation: where the theme is spoken, and where it is still unspoken.
lesson.f6u6l1.part.expression: Use one sentence to say the next action.
lesson.f6u6l1.part.making: The review will not be written as an administrative submission procedure, and will not write a school-year timetable.
lesson.f6u6l2.part.element: The overview should be able to say what the artwork / critical studies present.
lesson.f6u6l2.part.principle: A four-sentence structure: one theme sentence, what the research workbook has done, what the artwork / critical studies present, and what the next step is. The two parts should support each other.
lesson.f6u6l2.part.appreciate: Object of appreciation: the draft of your Form 6 portfolio overview. Focus of appreciation: which workbook page corresponds to which decision in the work.
lesson.f6u6l2.part.expression: Use four sentences to say the theme, the process, the presentation and the next step.
lesson.f6u6l2.part.making: There is no locked word count. It is enough that each of the four sentences does one job.

lesson.f4u3l3.appr.left.title: Piazza San Marco
lesson.f4u3l3.appr.left.source: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, NY
lesson.f4u3l3.appr.left.intro: The piazza is organised by the paved floor and the arcades on both sides, with the basilica and campanile closing the far end. Tiny figures walk or gather across the open square. The painting presents a Venetian public place as a space of everyday meeting and passage.
lesson.f4u3l3.appr.right.title: Fireworks at Ryōgoku Bridge, from the series One Hundred Famous Views of Edo
lesson.f4u3l3.appr.right.source: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, NY
lesson.f4u3l3.appr.right.intro: The upper half is night sky, with fireworks and smoke opening out; the lower half is the river, boats, and lights along both banks. Many small spectators gather on the bridge and in the boats. The print presents Ryōgoku Bridge in Edo as a public place where people watch a summer night display together.
lesson.f4u3l4.appr.left.title: The Third-Class Carriage
lesson.f4u3l4.appr.left.source: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, NY
lesson.f4u3l4.appr.left.intro: In the carriage, three travellers sit close in the foreground; their bodies and a basket fill much of the picture, with more figures behind. Light enters from a window at the left, and the poses stay quiet. The painting presents a third-class public train compartment as a situation where ordinary people travel together.
lesson.f4u3l4.appr.right.title: The Horse Fair
lesson.f4u3l4.appr.right.source: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, NY
lesson.f4u3l4.appr.right.intro: The large canvas spreads a controlled yet running herd of horses from left to right, with riders and handlers woven into a diagonal movement. Dust on the ground and a line of trees at the back mark an outdoor site. The painting presents a Paris horse market as a public place of sale, strength, and skill.
